seo_title: Seasonal Charcuterie Board Ideas: 25 Boards for Every Season
description: 25 seasonal charcuterie board ideas for fall, winter, spring and summer: fall harvest, Friendsgiving, Christmas, hot cocoa, Easter, summer backyard and picnic boards, plus what's in season for each.
answer: A seasonal charcuterie board follows what's at the market: pears, figs, apples and aged cheddar in fall; bold aged cheeses, cranberries, rosemary and spiced nuts in winter; strawberries, snap peas, radishes and fresh goat cheese in spring; and peaches, melon, berries and hard cheeses that hold up in the heat in summer. Here are 25 ideas, season by season.
intro: The easiest way to make a board feel special is to build it around what's in season. The fruit tastes better, it costs less, and the colors on the board match the time of year without any decorations.
The ideas below start with fall and winter, when most people make boards, and link to each holiday's own page of ideas.

sections.heading: What's in season for a charcuterie board

items.text: pears, apples, figs, grapes, pomegranate, pumpkin seeds and pecans. Aged cheddar, Gruyère, Gorgonzola and smoked Gouda. Fig jam, apple butter and quince paste.
cranberries, citrus, pomegranate and dried fruit. Stilton, aged Gouda, Comté and baked brie. Spiced nuts, dark honey and rosemary.
strawberries, snap peas, radishes, asparagus and fresh herbs. Fresh goat cheese, burrata and ricotta. Honey and strawberry jam.
peaches, cherries, melon, berries, cucumbers and cherry tomatoes. Parmigiano, aged Manchego and feta, which hold up in the heat. Basil and pesto.

sections.heading: How to make any board seasonal
paras: You don't need a new board for every season. Keep the cheese and meat you like and change four things: the fruit, the jam, the nut and the herb. A classic board with pears, fig jam, candied pecans and rosemary is a fall board. The same board with peaches, honey, almonds and basil is a summer board.
For a full plan built around your guest count, use the [Party Planner](/party-planner/), or start from the [Board Builder](/board-builder/).

sections.heading: Summer boards and food safety
paras: Cheese, meat and dips shouldn't sit out for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour when it's above 90°F. Outdoors in summer, put out smaller amounts, keep the rest in a cooler or the fridge, and refill. Hard cheeses like Parmigiano and aged Manchego hold up better in the heat than brie.

items.text: Winter peaches and summer pears are expensive and bland. Build around what's in season.
Brie and fresh cheeses slump and spoil faster in the heat. Swap in hard, aged cheeses.
Let the season's fruit, herbs and colors do the work. Plastic leaves and ornaments just take up space.

items.lead: Planning a holiday board too late.
items.text: Specialty cheese for Thanksgiving and Christmas can sell out. Order it a week ahead.

faq.q: What goes on a fall charcuterie board?
faq.a: Aged cheddar, Gruyère or Gorgonzola, prosciutto or soppressata, pears, figs, apples, pomegranate, dried cranberries, candied walnuts or pecans, and fig jam or apple butter.

faq.q: What goes on a winter charcuterie board?
faq.a: Bold aged cheeses like Stilton, aged Gouda and Comté, rich cured meats, dried cranberries, spiced nuts, dark honey, fig jam and rosemary.

faq.q: What goes on a spring charcuterie board?
faq.a: Fresh goat cheese, burrata or ricotta, prosciutto, strawberries, snap peas, radishes, fresh herbs, honey and strawberry jam.

faq.q: What goes on a summer charcuterie board?
faq.a: Peaches, melon, cherries and berries, prosciutto or bresaola, and hard cheeses like Parmigiano and aged Manchego that hold up in the heat.

faq.q: How long can a charcuterie board sit out in summer?
faq.a: No more than 1 hour when it's above 90°F, and 2 hours otherwise. Put out small amounts and refill from a cooler or the fridge.

faq.q: How do I make a charcuterie board feel seasonal without starting over?
faq.a: Keep your usual cheese and meat and swap four things: the fruit, the jam, the nut and the herb. Pears, fig jam, pecans and rosemary say fall; peaches, honey, almonds and basil say summer.
